t: Building Boxes - Triangular Numbers in a Corner
o: You must place n unit cubes in a cubical room where a cube may rest on top of another only if all four vertical faces of the supporting cube touch another cube or a wall; the goal is to minimize how many cubes touch the floor. Huddling everything into a corner is always optimal, because two wall faces then support columns for free. The samples reveal the growth pattern: for n = 4 the footprint is a corner trio of cells holding heights 2, 1, 1 (answer 3), and for n = 10 a complete corner pyramid with base side 3 packs 1 + 3 + 6 = 10 cubes on just 6 floor cubes. Quantitatively, a complete pyramid of base side L holds the tetrahedral number L(L+1)(L+2)/6 boxes on an L(L+1)/2 triangular footprint, and leftover boxes continue along the next diagonal of the footprint in groups of 1, 3, 6, ... boxes that cost only 1, 2, 3, ... new floor cells. Since n reaches a billion, we resolve those formulas arithmetically instead of simulating box by box.
k: Corner placement is optimal: every wall face is free support, and the best footprint is always a corner staircase of triangular layers.

Complete pyramids follow tetrahedral counts L(L+1)(L+2)/6 on triangular footprints L(L+1)/2; leftovers pack along the next diagonal where groups of tri(j) = j(j+1)/2 boxes share just j new floor cells.
Products like (L+1)(L+2)(L+3) reach about 10^10 when n = 10^9, so fixed-width languages need 64-bit arithmetic throughout.

a.i: Grow the largest complete corner pyramid that fits: keep adding layers while their tetrahedral total stays within n. Let the remainder be r and find the largest j with j(j+1)/2 <= r; those boxes occupy exactly j extra floor cells along the next diagonal, and if any boxes are still left over one further floor cell absorbs the tail. The answer is tri(L) + j, plus one when a tail exists.
s: Find the largest L with L(L+1)(L+2)/6 <= n and subtract that count from n.
On the remainder r, find the largest j with j(j+1)/2 <= r.
Answer = L(L+1)/2 + j, plus 1 if r - j(j+1)/2 is still positive.
a.t: O(n^(1/3) + sqrt(n)) - the layer loop runs until the tetrahedral count passes n and the diagonal loop until a triangular number passes the remainder.

a.i: Both tetra(L) = L(L+1)(L+2)/6 and tri(j) = j(j+1)/2 are monotone increasing, so the two scans of Approach 1 can each become a binary search. Same construction and answer, but O(log n) time regardless of how large n grows - mostly a robustness upgrade that removes any concern about loop iteration counts.
s: Binary-search the largest L in [0, 2000] with tetra(L) <= n; set r = n - tetra(L).
Binary-search the largest j in [0, 50000] with tri(j) <= r.
Return tri(L) + j, plus 1 if r - tri(j) > 0.
a.t: O(log n) - two binary searches over ranges of size O(n^(1/3)) and O(sqrt(n)).

w: Present Approach 1 and mention binary search as polish. The hard part is justifying the packing lemmas - sketch an exchange argument showing moving boxes toward the walls never increases floor contact, so the staircase-in-a-corner configuration dominates. Pitfalls: silent 32-bit overflow in the cubic term (use long / long long); forgetting that a leftover partial group still needs one extra floor cell; and assuming leftovers can simply extend the top layer - a column may grow only when all four faces of its new supporter are sealed, which is why extras go on the next diagonal instead. Follow-ups: invert the formulas to compute the maximum box count for a given floor budget F, or handle rooms with only one wall.
